summary:
Greater Poland Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and the sources document no voivodeship-specific deviation from it. Entry is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, and lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence; the Border Guard refused to move or release her regardless, and she was freed only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication. The case also documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying hormone replacement therapy to a trans prisoner held in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged Article 3 and Article 14 breaches undecided, but held that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and is the governing standard for trans healthcare in Polish custody, including in Greater Poland Voivodeship. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

The protective legal layer is unsettled. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.
tangentialFactors:
The two hard findings point in opposite directions. The 11 July 2024 judgment shows medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, but the award was EUR 8,000 and the Article 3 claim failed, so the remedy arrives after the harm rather than preventing it.

The March 2024 detention case turned on NGO intervention, not on the statutory bar operating on its own: the legal protection existed on paper and the Border Guard disregarded it until a legal-aid association applied to the post commander. A trans visitor without that backing enters the same procedure with less leverage.

Foreigner status compounds exposure. The Canadian advisory lists it alongside sexual orientation as a reported motive for harassment, and the documented detention victim was herself a foreign national on hormone therapy, so the intersection of trans status and non-citizen status is where the sourced harm sits.

Legislative turbulence cuts both ways: a hate-speech amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI violence was cleared in May 2024 but approval was postponed, with a second bill in late October, so the strength of protection at any given moment depends on bills whose passage is not settled.

Partnership recognition is the area of clearest movement, with the June 2024 directive reversal and the September 2024 Strasbourg ruling, but neither source states that a recognition framework has since been enacted.
localsOnly:
The statutory placement bar applies to residents as well as visitors: Polish law prohibits placing a person in a guarded centre wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence, and the March 2024 case shows the bar being invoked for a trans woman in immigration detention.

Residents in Polish prisons fall under the 11 July 2024 European Court of Human Rights standard, which requires hormone replacement therapy not be withheld without reasonable legal grounds; Poland runs no specialised trans prison section, so placement within Greater Poland Voivodeship's facilities is decided case by case.

Resident couples remain affected by the absence of a partnership framework: the September 2024 ruling characterised that absence as an illegal vacuum, while the June 2024 revocation of the Ziobro directive only restored recognition of marriage certificates obtained abroad.

Residents reporting anti-trans abuse depend on a protection regime still in flux, with the Prosecutor General's special response team and its law-enforcement guidelines operating alongside bills whose approval was postponed.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not identify which voivodeship's court handled the 13 March 2024 detention case; the inventory treats it as governing here, but the geographic link is not stated in the case report itself and remains unresolved.

The status of the March and October 2024 hate-speech bills at the time of travel is not sourced and should be verified rather than assumed.

No voivodeship-level data is sourced on local detention capacity, prison healthcare provision, or access to gender-affirming care in Greater Poland Voivodeship; the record relies on national and Strasbourg-level findings.

The European Court of Human Rights left the Article 3 and Article 14 allegations in the prison case undecided, so no finding on inhuman treatment or discrimination in that matter exists.

Whether Poland has enacted a partnership recognition framework following the September 2024 ruling is not stated in the inventory.
